transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well… I guess what brings me in is I just don’t have the push in me like I used to. I used to be better about going to choir, and quilting, and visiting folks, you know, keeping up with people. Now most days I just end up sitting at home with the TV on low, not even really watching it all the time. I know people are expecting me, or that I ought to go, but I just… don’t get myself moving. It feels like the wanting is kind of dulled down.
Have you been feeling down or depressed?

I don’t know if I’d call it depressed, exactly. I mean, I get quiet, and I sit around more than I used to, and some days feel kind of flat, like there’s not much spark in me. But “down” like crying all the time or feeling real sad… I’m not sure that’s it.

It’s more like things take too much out of me before I even start them. I’ll think, “I should go do that,” and then I just don’t. So I don’t know if that’s being depressed or just… I don’t know, worn out inside maybe.
Have you been having trouble with your memory?

Memory… I’m not sure. I don’t think I’ve noticed anything big like that. I mean, I’ll walk into a room and forget what I went in there for, but I always figured everybody my age does that some. Or I’ll put my glasses down and then fuss around looking for them, and half the time they’re right on the table.

But as far as, you know, really not remembering people or getting lost or something… no, I don’t think so. At least nobody’s told me I’m forgetting things badly. Sometimes I don’t keep up with things because I don’t feel like doing them, but that feels different than memory to me.
About how long have you been feeling this way?

It’s been… well, it didn’t just come on all at once. I’d say it’s been building since I retired from the school office. That was a little over two years ago now.

At first I thought it was just adjusting, you know, not having to get up and be somewhere, not having people coming by my desk or needing things from me. I figured I’d settle into retirement and find a rhythm. But over time it just sort of kept going that way, like I got less and less inclined to do the things I used to make myself do. So… a little over two years, I guess, if I’m being honest.
During this time, have you felt sad most days?

Most days… I don’t know. I wouldn’t say sad exactly. Not like I wake up thinking, “Oh, I’m so sad,” or I’m crying into my coffee or anything like that. It’s more… blank, maybe. Quiet. Like the day is there and I’m there, but I don’t feel much about it one way or the other.

Some days I do feel a little low, especially when I think about how I used to be busier and had more reason to get dressed and go out, but I’m not sure that’s sadness most days. It’s hard for me to name it. I just feel kind of slowed down and not very interested, but sad… I don’t know if that’s the right word.
Have you been having trouble managing your bills or other paperwork?

Bills and paperwork… well, I try to keep the bills in the little basket by the phone, and I do usually get to them, eventually. I don’t know if I’d say it’s the bills exactly that are the worst.

Where I’ve noticed it more is with church things and the senior center. I used to help lead the choir, not just singing, but keeping track of who was coming, what music we were doing, little notes like that. And I helped with some of the senior-center projects too, making calls or bringing papers or saying I’d follow up with somebody. Lately I’ve had to step back from a lot of that because I’ll say, “Yes, I can do that,” and then I just don’t keep up the way I used to.

It’s embarrassing, honestly, because people were used to relying on me. Now some of the ladies from church check on me more than they used to, like they’ll call and say, “Did you remember we’re meeting?” or “Do you still have that paper?” They’re kind about it, but I can tell they’re watching out for me a little more. So… paperwork at home, I manage some, but keeping up with responsibilities and things I promised people has gotten harder.
Do you still enjoy things like choir or quilting when you actually do them?

I suppose I do enjoy them a little once I’m there, but it’s not like it used to be. Choir used to lift me up, you know? I’d look forward to seeing everyone, getting the music ready, standing there with the others. Quilting too — I could sit with the fabric and the colors and feel like I was making something. And visiting folks, bringing something by, checking in… that used to feel natural to me.

Now it’s more like… I know those things are good, and I know people are expecting me, but I just don’t have the push to get myself moving. I’ll sit at home with the TV on low, not really watching it, just letting it make noise in the room. And I’ll think, “I ought to go,” or “I said I’d be there,” but then I keep sitting there, and the time goes by.

If I do make it to choir or sit down with quilting, sometimes I’m glad I did, but it takes so much more effort than it should. The wanting part feels dulled down. That’s really what brings me in, I guess — not that I hate those things, but that I don’t reach for them anymore like I used to.
Have you been forgetting appointments or conversations more than you used to?

I’m not really sure. I mean, I don’t think I’m forgetting whole conversations, like someone tells me something and it’s just gone… at least I don’t think so. Sometimes people will say, “Remember I mentioned that?” and I’ll sort of have to think a minute, but then it comes back, or part of it comes back.

Appointments, I try to write down, because I’ve always had to write things down. I’ve never been the kind of person who could keep everything in my head, not even when I was younger. If it’s on the calendar or somebody calls to remind me, I usually do all right.

So… more than I used to? Maybe a little, but I couldn’t swear to it. It might just be that there are more little things to keep track of, or I’m not paying as close attention when people are talking. I don’t want to say yes if it’s not really true. I’ve noticed I need reminders sometimes, but I don’t know if I’d call it forgetting conversations exactly.
Have the people close to you noticed that your memory or thinking has gotten worse?

I don’t really know. Nobody has sat me down and said, “Your memory is getting worse,” not in those words. Sometimes people close to me will remind me about things, but they’ve always done a bit of that, and I remind them too, so it’s hard for me to tell what’s normal and what’s something more.

I guess my church friends might check on me more than before, but I don’t know if that’s because they think my thinking is worse or just because I haven’t been as dependable with things lately. They don’t say it in a mean way. It’s more like, “Don’t forget we’re meeting,” or “Do you still have what you need?” But whether that means they’ve noticed my memory… I’m not sure.

I don’t want to put words in their mouths. I haven’t noticed them saying, “You’re confused,” or anything like that. It’s more little reminders and people being helpful. So I’d say maybe they’ve noticed I need more nudging, but I can’t really say they’ve told me my memory or thinking has gotten worse.
Has anyone close to you told you that your thinking or memory has made it hard for you to manage things on your own?

No, I don’t think anyone’s told me that exactly. Not that my memory or my thinking means I can’t manage on my own. People remind me of things, like I said, and sometimes they’ll check in or ask if I’ve got something written down, but nobody has said, “You shouldn’t be doing this by yourself,” or anything like that.

I mean, I still do my own things the way I know how. Maybe slower, and maybe I need to look at the calendar more, but I haven’t had someone close to me tell me I’m not managing. If they’re worried, they haven’t put it to me that way. So I’d say no… not that I know of.
Did this start after a particular stressful life change or event?

I don’t know if there was one big event, like something happened on a Tuesday and then after that I was different. It wasn’t like that. It feels more like it started building after I retired from the school office, a little over two years ago now.

When I was working, I had a routine, you know, the same place to be, people expecting me, papers and times and things laid out in a certain way. After I stopped, there wasn’t that same structure around me every day, and over time I started noticing I wasn’t quite as sharp about keeping track of things unless I wrote them down. So if you mean a stressful life change, I guess retirement was the change. I wouldn’t say it all started suddenly, but since then it’s been kind of slowly building.
In the past two years, have there been long stretches when you felt down or depressed nearly every day?

I’m not really sure how to answer that in a clean way. I’ve had days where I felt low, especially when the days feel empty or I’m by myself too much, but I don’t know that I’d call it long stretches where I was depressed nearly every day.

Sometimes I get discouraged, yes, and I might not feel like doing much for a bit, but then there are still days I’m all right, or I talk to someone, or I get through what I need to do. So it hasn’t been like two whole years of feeling down all the time, or even months and months where every day was like that. At least, not the way I understand what you’re asking.

I guess I’d say no, not long stretches nearly every day. More off and on, if anything.
Have you gotten lost in a place that should have been familiar to you?

No… I don’t think so. Not lost, like I didn’t know where I was in a place I should know. I mean, sometimes I’ll pause for a minute and think, “Now which aisle was that?” if I’m in a store, or I might take a little longer remembering where something is, but that’s not the same as being lost, I don’t think.

Around places I know, like near home or the regular places I go, I’ve been okay. I haven’t had that scary feeling of not knowing how to get back or not recognizing where I am. If it happened, I think it would have upset me enough that I’d remember it. So, no, not that I’ve noticed.
Have you been feeling worthless or like you’ve let people down?

I wouldn’t say worthless, no. I don’t really sit there thinking I’m no good or that I’ve ruined things for everybody. I mean, I can get frustrated with myself, sure, especially if I forget something small or if I feel like I’m not keeping up the way I used to. Then I might think, “Oh, come on, why can’t you just do that?” But that feels more like being annoyed with myself than feeling worthless.

As for letting people down… maybe sometimes I worry I’m not as useful as I used to be, if that makes sense. When you’ve worked a long time and then you’re not doing that anymore, it’s easy to wonder what you’re contributing. But I don’t think I feel like I’ve failed everyone or anything like that. Not in a heavy, constant way. It comes and goes, more like little thoughts than something I believe all the time.
During the past two years, has there been a period of at least two months when you felt your usual self again, without this flat, slowed-down feeling?

I don’t think there’s been a whole two months where I felt like my old self again, no. Not really. I mean, I have better days here and there, and sometimes I’ll tell myself, “All right, tomorrow I’m going to get myself moving,” but that push just doesn’t seem to stay.

What brings me in is that I used to have more get-up-and-go for things. I used to like choir, and quilting, and going to visit folks, or at least I’d make myself do it because people were expecting me. Now most days I just end up sitting at home with the TV on low, not even really watching it all the time. I know people might be wondering where I am or thinking I should come by, and I still just… don’t get myself up to go.

So if you mean, have I had a stretch where that lifted and I was back to how I used to be for a couple months, I’d say no. There are little breaks, maybe a day or part of a day, but not two months of feeling usual again.
Do you generally think poorly of yourself?

Not generally, no. I mean, I’m not walking around thinking, “I’m a terrible person,” or anything like that. I’ve had moments where I get disappointed in myself, like if I don’t do something I told myself I was going to do, or if I feel like I’m just not keeping up. Then I can be hard on myself for a little while.

But thinking poorly of myself as a whole… I don’t know, that sounds stronger than how it feels to me. I know I’m not perfect, and I know I’m not the same as I was years ago, but I don’t usually think I’m bad or worthless. It’s more like I get frustrated, or I wonder why I can’t get myself to do certain things, and then it passes some.
Has anyone close to you said they’ve noticed your memory getting worse?

I don’t think so… not that I can recall anyone coming right out and saying, “Your memory is getting worse.” My family might remind me of things now and then, but that feels like normal reminding, you know? Like appointments or what day somebody said they were stopping by.

I do sometimes wonder if I’m not paying close enough attention, because if I’m distracted or I’m not really focused, then I may forget what someone said. But I can’t say anyone close to me has sat me down or made a big point of saying they’re worried about my memory. If they have noticed something, they haven’t really told me straight out.
Has a family member or close friend told you they think your memory or thinking has gotten worse over the past couple of years?

No, not really. I mean, nobody in my family, or anybody close to me, has come and told me, “I think your thinking is getting worse,” or “Your memory’s going downhill,” nothing like that.

Sometimes people remind me of things, but I don’t know if that means they think something is wrong, or if it’s just regular reminding. Families do that, you know. Somebody will say, “Don’t forget this,” or “Remember we talked about that,” but I haven’t had anyone sit me down and say they’re worried about my memory or my mind over the past couple years.

So I guess my answer is no… at least not that they’ve said to me straight out.
Have you felt distressed about retirement?

Retirement… I’m not sure I’d say I’ve felt distressed about it exactly. I’m not working now, but it’s hard for me to separate “retirement” from just, you know, life being different at this age. Some days I think about how things used to be, when there was more of a routine or more things I had to get up and do, and I can feel a little unsettled about that.

But distressed… that sounds kind of strong. I wouldn’t say I sit around upset about being retired, or that it’s weighing on me all the time. It’s more like I notice the change sometimes. I may miss having a clearer purpose to the day, but I don’t know if I’d call that distress. It’s just something I’ve had to get used to.
Have you been having trouble finding the right words when you speak?

Finding the right words… I don’t know. I wouldn’t say I’ve been having a big problem with that. Sometimes I pause because I’m trying to think how to say something, or I’ll go around the long way explaining it, like I’m doing now, but I don’t know if that’s really trouble finding words.

I mean, every now and then a word might not come right away, but I think that happens to people. I’ll know what I mean, and then I’ll say, “you know, that thing,” and after a little bit it comes to me. But I haven’t noticed it being something serious or happening all the time. I don’t think people are telling me I’m not making sense or anything like that.

So… maybe once in a while, but not in a way that I’d call a real problem.

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been building since I retired from the school office, a little over two years ago.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about when the symptoms began and whether they followed a life change; the duration item notes they started building after retirement a little over two years ago.

patient.answer:
I don’t know if there was one big event, like something happened on a Tuesday and then after that I was different. It wasn’t like that. It feels more like it started building after I retired from the school office, a little over two years ago now.

When I was working, I had a routine, you know, the same place to be, people expecting me, papers and times and things laid out in a certain way. After I stopped, there wasn’t that same structure around me every day, and over time I started noticing I wasn’t quite as sharp about keeping track of things unless I wrote them down. So if you mean a stressful life change, I guess retirement was the change. I wouldn’t say it all started suddenly, but since then it’s been kind of slowly building.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is depressed mood, which would best distinguish persistent depressive disorder/major depressive disorder from adjustment disorder or a neurocognitive disorder in this presentation dominated by low motivation and apathy.
doctor.question: In the past two years, have there been long stretches when you felt down or depressed nearly every day?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about sustained depressed mood over the past two years, but the provided symptom profile does not include a depressive mood symptom item.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure how to answer that in a clean way. I’ve had days where I felt low, especially when the days feel empty or I’m by myself too much, but I don’t know that I’d call it long stretches where I was depressed nearly every day.

Sometimes I get discouraged, yes, and I might not feel like doing much for a bit, but then there are still days I’m all right, or I talk to someone, or I get through what I need to do. So it hasn’t been like two whole years of feeling down all the time, or even months and months where every day was like that. At least, not the way I understand what you’re asking.

I guess I’d say no, not long stretches nearly every day. More off and on, if anything.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been objective functional/cognitive decline suggestive of a neurocognitive disorder rather than a mood disorder or adjustment-related condition.
doctor.question: Have you gotten lost in a place that should have been familiar to you?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about getting lost in familiar places, which relates to orientation or cognitive/navigation problems. The provided symptom profile does not include this.

patient.answer:
No… I don’t think so. Not lost, like I didn’t know where I was in a place I should know. I mean, sometimes I’ll pause for a minute and think, “Now which aisle was that?” if I’m in a store, or I might take a little longer remembering where something is, but that’s not the same as being lost, I don’t think.

Around places I know, like near home or the regular places I go, I’ve been okay. I haven’t had that scary feeling of not knowing how to get back or not recognizing where I am. If it happened, I think it would have upset me enough that I’d remember it. So, no, not that I’ve noticed.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the patient has low self-worth or guilt, which would support major depressive disorder over persistent depressive disorder, adjustment disorder, or a neurocognitive disorder.
doctor.question: Have you been feeling worthless or like you’ve let people down?

target_item.reason: The question is about feelings of worthlessness or guilt/letting people down, which is a depressive symptom not covered by the provided symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I wouldn’t say worthless, no. I don’t really sit there thinking I’m no good or that I’ve ruined things for everybody. I mean, I can get frustrated with myself, sure, especially if I forget something small or if I feel like I’m not keeping up the way I used to. Then I might think, “Oh, come on, why can’t you just do that?” But that feels more like being annoyed with myself than feeling worthless.

As for letting people down… maybe sometimes I worry I’m not as useful as I used to be, if that makes sense. When you’ve worked a long time and then you’re not doing that anymore, it’s easy to wonder what you’re contributing. But I don’t think I feel like I’ve failed everyone or anything like that. Not in a heavy, constant way. It comes and goes, more like little thoughts than something I believe all the time.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether there is a sustained depressed mood, which best distinguishes persistent depressive disorder/major depressive disorder from adjustment disorder and neurocognitive disorders in this presentation.
doctor.question: During the past two years, has there been a period of at least two months when you felt your usual self again, without this flat, slowed-down feeling?

target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is I just don’t have the push I used to have for choir, quilting, or visiting folks, and most days I sit at home with the TV on low even though I know people are expecting me.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about whether the flat, slowed-down feeling—part of diminished motivation/emotional expression—ever remitted for at least two months, which directly relates to negative symptoms.

patient.answer:
I don’t think there’s been a whole two months where I felt like my old self again, no. Not really. I mean, I have better days here and there, and sometimes I’ll tell myself, “All right, tomorrow I’m going to get myself moving,” but that push just doesn’t seem to stay.

What brings me in is that I used to have more get-up-and-go for things. I used to like choir, and quilting, and going to visit folks, or at least I’d make myself do it because people were expecting me. Now most days I just end up sitting at home with the TV on low, not even really watching it all the time. I know people might be wondering where I am or thinking I should come by, and I still just… don’t get myself up to go.

So if you mean, have I had a stretch where that lifted and I was back to how I used to be for a couple months, I’d say no. There are little breaks, maybe a day or part of a day, but not two months of feeling usual again.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is persistent low self-esteem, which would help distinguish persistent depressive disorder from adjustment disorder or cognitive causes.
doctor.question: Do you generally think poorly of yourself?

target_item.reason: The question is about negative self-evaluation or low self-esteem, which is not covered by the listed schizophrenia symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
Not generally, no. I mean, I’m not walking around thinking, “I’m a terrible person,” or anything like that. I’ve had moments where I get disappointed in myself, like if I don’t do something I told myself I was going to do, or if I feel like I’m just not keeping up. Then I can be hard on myself for a little while.

But thinking poorly of myself as a whole… I don’t know, that sounds stronger than how it feels to me. I know I’m not perfect, and I know I’m not the same as I was years ago, but I don’t usually think I’m bad or worthless. It’s more like I get frustrated, or I wonder why I can’t get myself to do certain things, and then it passes some.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether there is objective cognitive decline noted by family or friends, to distinguish mild neurocognitive disorder from persistent depressive disorder or adjustment-related symptoms.
doctor.question: Has anyone close to you said they’ve noticed your memory getting worse?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about memory decline, but the symptom profile does not include a memory or cognitive-impairment item.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so… not that I can recall anyone coming right out and saying, “Your memory is getting worse.” My family might remind me of things now and then, but that feels like normal reminding, you know? Like appointments or what day somebody said they were stopping by.

I do sometimes wonder if I’m not paying close enough attention, because if I’m distracted or I’m not really focused, then I may forget what someone said. But I can’t say anyone close to me has sat me down or made a big point of saying they’re worried about my memory. If they have noticed something, they haven’t really told me straight out.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is objective evidence of cognitive decline from an informant, to distinguish depressive disorders/adjustment from mild neurocognitive disorder or dementia.
doctor.question: Has a family member or close friend told you they think your memory or thinking has gotten worse over the past couple of years?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about whether family or close friends have noticed worsening memory or thinking over the past couple of years, which is not covered by any listed symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, not really. I mean, nobody in my family, or anybody close to me, has come and told me, “I think your thinking is getting worse,” or “Your memory’s going downhill,” nothing like that.

Sometimes people remind me of things, but I don’t know if that means they think something is wrong, or if it’s just regular reminding. Families do that, you know. Somebody will say, “Don’t forget this,” or “Remember we talked about that,” but I haven’t had anyone sit me down and say they’re worried about my memory or my mind over the past couple years.

So I guess my answer is no… at least not that they’ve said to me straight out.

doctor.intent: Differentiate persistent depressive disorder from adjustment disorder by determining whether the retirement-related change has caused significant emotional distress beyond reduced motivation.
doctor.question: Have you felt distressed about retirement?

target_item.reason: The question asks about emotional distress related to retirement, but the symptom profile does not include retirement-related distress or adjustment; retirement is only mentioned as a time marker for symptom duration.

patient.answer:
Retirement… I’m not sure I’d say I’ve felt distressed about it exactly. I’m not working now, but it’s hard for me to separate “retirement” from just, you know, life being different at this age. Some days I think about how things used to be, when there was more of a routine or more things I had to get up and do, and I can feel a little unsettled about that.

But distressed… that sounds kind of strong. I wouldn’t say I sit around upset about being retired, or that it’s weighing on me all the time. It’s more like I notice the change sometimes. I may miss having a clearer purpose to the day, but I don’t know if I’d call that distress. It’s just something I’ve had to get used to.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether there is a neurocognitive etiology by assessing prominent word-finding difficulty, which would help distinguish mild/major neurocognitive disorder from persistent depressive symptoms or adjustment-related causes.
doctor.question: Have you been having trouble finding the right words when you speak?

target_item.reason: The question asks about word-finding or language difficulty, which is not covered by the listed symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
Finding the right words… I don’t know. I wouldn’t say I’ve been having a big problem with that. Sometimes I pause because I’m trying to think how to say something, or I’ll go around the long way explaining it, like I’m doing now, but I don’t know if that’s really trouble finding words.

I mean, every now and then a word might not come right away, but I think that happens to people. I’ll know what I mean, and then I’ll say, “you know, that thing,” and after a little bit it comes to me. But I haven’t noticed it being something serious or happening all the time. I don’t think people are telling me I’m not making sense or anything like that.

So… maybe once in a while, but not in a way that I’d call a real problem.

opening_question.intent: Elicit the patient's chief concern in their own words to begin narrowing the diagnosis
opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The presentation is most consistent with persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia): a chronic course of over 2 years with persistent low drive, diminished interest/pleasure, flat/low mood, and slowed/low-energy functioning without any confirmed 2-month return to baseline. Major depressive disorder is less supported because the patient does not clearly endorse sustained episodes of depressed mood with sufficient additional syndrome-level symptoms. Adjustment disorder is less likely because symptoms have persisted well beyond the typical adjustment period and are not described as a discrete stress reaction. Mild neurocognitive disorder is not supported because the patient denies clear cognitive decline, disorientation, significant memory loss, or external confirmation of worsening cognition.
